items.followUp: Define a saturated solution and give one example.

rubric.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the mixture as homogeneous or uniform.

rubric.why: A suitable example shows a solute dissolved in a solvent.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a correct solute–solvent example.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
In a sugar solution, sugar is dissolved in water.

items.followUp: State the rule ‘like dissolves like’ and give one example involving a non-polar solvent.

rubric.why: The rule means substances with similar polarity dissolve one another.
rubric.description: Explains the meaning of ‘like dissolves like’.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar substances in non-polar solvents.

rubric.why: A correct example applies the rule to a solute and solvent of similar character.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as sugar dissolving in water or iodine dissolving in carbon tetrachloride.

modelAnswer: ‘Like dissolves like’ means that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, while non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.
For example, polar sugar dissolves in polar water.

items.followUp: Write any two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Any valid physical property earns credit.
rubric.description: Gives one correct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one valid property, such as being brittle or a poor conductor of heat or electricity.

rubric.why: A second distinct property completes the response.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different valid property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally brittle in the solid state.
They are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.

items.followUp: Name the elements in Group 1 of the periodic table.

rubric.why: The response must identify halogens from Group 17 (VIIA).
rubric.description: Names at least three halogens correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any three correct names from fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.

rubric.why: Listing the complete group demonstrates full recall of the elements.
rubric.description: Names all five commonly listed halogens.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for listing fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.

modelAnswer: The halogens are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.

items.followUp: Write any five properties of electrons.

rubric.why: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles.
rubric.description: Identifies the negative charge or electron nature of cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are negatively charged or consist of electrons.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays are deflected by a field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming an electric or magnetic field and stating that the rays are deflected.

rubric.why: Cathode rays produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays produce fluorescence or a glow.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Their nature does not depend on the gas in the tube or the material of the electrodes.
rubric.description: States that cathode-ray properties are independent of the gas or electrode material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either independence.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
They consist of negatively charged particles called electrons.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
Their nature is independent of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.

items.followUp: Define any four branches of chemistry other than those named in your answer.

rubric.why: Physical chemistry deals with the physical properties and changes of matter, including energy changes.
rubric.description: Defines physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition involving physical properties or changes of matter and energy.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Defines organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying carbon compounds as its subject.

rubric.why: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Defines inorganic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying elements and their compounds as its subject.

rubric.why: Analytical chemistry identifies substances and determines their composition or amounts.
rubric.description: Defines analytical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition involving identification or determination of the composition or amount of substances.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry deals with the physical properties and changes of matter and the energy changes involved.
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry is the study of elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Analytical chemistry deals with identifying substances and determining their composition.

items.followUp: Explain ionic bonding and describe two types of covalent bonds with examples.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pairs.
rubric.description: Explains the formation of a covalent bond by sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for sharing electrons and 1 for stating that the shared electrons form one or more pairs.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Describes a single covalent bond and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one shared pair and a correct example such as H₂ or Cl₂.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Describes a double covalent bond and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two shared pairs and a correct example such as O₂.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Describes a triple covalent bond and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for three shared pairs and a correct example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair of electrons; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs of electrons; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs of electrons; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Define crystalline and amorphous solids and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a regular, orderly pattern.
rubric.description: Describes the particle arrangement in a crystalline solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its particles have a regular or orderly arrangement.

rubric.why: A valid example identifies a crystalline solid.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a crystalline solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example such as sodium chloride or quartz.

rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack a regular, long-range arrangement of particles.
rubric.description: Describes the particle arrangement in an amorphous solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its particles lack a regular arrangement.

rubric.why: A valid example identifies an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: Gives an example of an amorphous solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example such as glass, plastic, rubber or wax.

modelAnswer: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a regular, orderly pattern; sodium chloride is an example.
Amorphous solids do not have a regular arrangement of particles; glass is an example.
